source.title: Frame-Conditioned Moral Computation in LLaMA 3.1-8B-Instruct: An Exploratory Mechanistic Interpretability Audit of Ethical Reasoning
source.authors: Ali Dasdan; Manan Shah; W. R. Neuman; Chad Coleman; K. Meghani; Safinah Ali

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses polysemanticity and uses neuron descriptions in an observational audit, but its results do not test whether neuron poles have one main job, whether explanations predict held-out activations, or whether neurons suffice as circuit units.
record.gate_note: The paper measures ethics-description prevalence, ranking, and activation in surfaced neuron rows. These are not measures of whether each pole has a coherent main job or whether its explanation predicts firing on new examples. It also does not report the Transluce simulator scores as a result. The cited discussion of other mechanistic studies is not a result of this paper. Behavioral verdicts and cluster metrics are not included because they do not measure the claim’s neuron-interpretability propositions.
record.test_reason: The study uses Transluce's simulator-scored neuron descriptions as a classification tool to label neurons as ethics-related, and measures prevalence and ranking of those labels on moral prompts in Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct. It reports no result on whether neuron poles have one main job, whether descriptions predict held-out activations, the share of interpretable neurons, or neuron-based circuit sufficiency. It explicitly did not verify descriptions on its prompts. This is reliance on the description pipeline as a tool (T4), not a test; 'discusses'/T6 understates its dependence on neuron descriptions.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors report similar ethics-label prevalence (~5%) with higher ranking in trolley batteries, situational anchoring of top descriptions to prompt vocabulary, and mixed coded verdicts. They also report no detected B4-vs-B5 ranking difference. They offer frame-conditioned moral computation as a hypothesis and propose 'mechanistic alignment' as a criterion. Causal contribution is left to intervention studies.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Transluce’s surfaced neuron descriptions and normalized scores with a dictionary-based ethics label; it does not test whether explanations predict activations on held-out examples or perform the original audit’s pole-level job classification.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt battery changes the ranking metrics: the trolley batteries have median First Rank 3 versus 9 in B1 and B3. The authors also report that relabeling L16/N3837 changes the trolley ranking summaries. Main analysis uses T=0.5; an earlier B1 collection across temperatures uses a different extraction floor and classifier and is not directly comparable.

fits_no_version.finding: Ethics-labeled descriptions are ~5% of retained neuron rows in all four batteries (5.12–5.67%), but rank higher in trolley batteries (median first rank 3 vs 9; Top-10 Density ~0.20 vs 0.10; Priority Ratio ~0.69 vs ~0.45).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, ethics-labeled neuron descriptions have stable prevalence across moral prompt types while their ranking rises for concrete trolley dilemmas.

record.code_released: Supplementary package accompanies the report; URL not stated.
record.problems: One model only; small hand-written prompt sets; one retained generation per prompt; neuron and cluster views come from separate generations; ethics labels rely on AI-generated descriptions and a dictionary without independent human validation or false-negative estimates. The authors did not verify descriptions on these moral prompts and did not run interventions. No matched non-moral controls.
record.rows_left_out: Behavioral verdicts and confidence, cluster-level metrics, and top-list similarity were left out because they do not measure the neuron-job or explanation-validation claims. The temperature collection uses an earlier pipeline and classifier and is not directly comparable.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B pole-level job shares (≈90% one job, ≈7% two related, 2–4% not understood).
Shares across other dense/MoE models and scale; only Llama 3.1-8B is used, and no job shares are measured.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization versus superposition (paper only cites superposition as background).
Whether interpretable share rises with tools or architecture; vision-model estimates.
Neuron-basis attribution graphs explaining behaviour without a replacement model; no circuit analysis or interventions.
Whether explanations fitting activating examples fail to predict firing; descriptions were not verified on the moral prompts.
Simulation scores on new text and the share of neurons scoring well; the pipeline's scoring is described but no scores are reported.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from discusses/T6 to uses_without_test/T4: the entire analysis depends on Transluce neuron descriptions (themselves simulator-scored) as a labeling tool, without evaluating their accuracy. The paper mentions polysemanticity (e.g. sports descriptions possibly standing for abstract features) only speculatively, with no measurement. The 'Noise' bucket (~58–62% of cluster membership) reflects dictionary coverage, not neuron interpretability, and should not be read as bearing on V1/V7.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit shares, including one-job, two-related-job, and not-understood proportions.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose interpretation, and recursive generalization.
Architecture/tool explanations, change with tools or architecture, and the InceptionV1-sized-model estimates.
Attribution graphs and whether model behavior can be explained without a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitting activating examples fail to predict where neurons fire.
Automated scoring of explanations by simulating activations on new text and the proportion reaching good scores.
